title: Wells Fargo Bank Minnesota, National Association v. B.C.B.U.
citation: 143 Cal. App. 4th 493, 49 Cal. Rptr. 3d 324 (2006), modified Oct. 27, 2006
lead: A nursing-home operator signed equipment-acceptance papers before any deal was complete. A qualified assignee could enforce the promised waiver of defenses even though the equipment never arrived and the original parties later rescinded.

actors.name: B.C.B.U.
actors.role: Utah nursing-home and in-home care operator

actors.name: Wells Fargo Bank Minnesota, National Association
actors.role: Trustee and assignee enforcing the lease and guaranty

proceedings: Trial on stipulated facts and declarations resulted in $107,656.24 plus interest against B.C.B.U. and enforcement of the guaranty.
Court of Appeal affirmed and awarded appellate costs; later modification added a statutory-timing footnote without changing judgment.
limits: Signed documentary acceptance was not actual delivery or acceptance: no equipment was delivered.
The court reserved forgery and applied the specific defenses and assignee qualifications on this record.

review.basis: Individually written and compared with the canonical full brief; no new independent opinion audit claimed.

sections.title: Unsigned details remain while signed papers enter commerce
sections.cue: Introduce the documents and their actual status.
paragraphs: In October 2000, B.C.B.U., which operated a Utah nursing home and in-home care service, began discussing computer-equipment financing with Crocker Capital. Crocker told its president, Dee R. Bangerter, that signing before completion was customary and that the papers would remain in escrow until agreement.

On November 22, Bangerter signed an undated lease, equipment-acceptance certificate, Schedule A, and personal guaranty. The lease allowed assignment and waived defenses, counterclaims and setoffs against an assignee that B.C.B.U. might have against the lessor. The certificate stated that the equipment had been received and accepted unconditionally. Beside the signature, however, a warning instructed the signer to wait for actual receipt and satisfaction.

On December 4, Crocker completed and dated the documents without authorization and assigned the lease and guaranty for approximately $99,000. The stipulated unauthorized dating was understood to include Crocker’s signature and December 4 date. The lease entered a securitized pool. Wells Fargo Bank Minnesota, National Association, acting as trustee, reviewed the pool December 8, found nothing amiss, and took assignment December 11.

B.C.B.U. and Crocker never reached their contemplated agreement. They rescinded January 30, 2001, and Crocker returned the first and last months’ payments. No equipment was ever delivered or actually accepted.

sections.title: The assignee enforces a separate waiver of defenses
sections.cue: Explain how the statutory protections fit together.
paragraphs: Wells Fargo sued in January 2003 for breach and declarations concerning the lease and guaranty. B.C.B.U. and Bangerter raised cancellation, failure of consideration and other defenses. B.C.B.U. later dismissed its cross-complaint against Crocker. After trial on stipulated facts and declarations, the judge enforced the waiver under California Uniform Commercial Code § 9403, awarding $107,656.24 plus interest against the company and declaring Bangerter’s guaranty enforceable.

On appeal, B.C.B.U. relied on § 10407, which makes promises in a nonconsumer finance lease irrevocable and independent upon acceptance. Since no goods had been accepted, it argued that enforcement failed. Acting Presiding Justice Bedsworth’s opinion, joined by Justices O’Leary and Ikola, explained that § 9403 supplied additional assignment protection.

That section allowed enforcement of a debtor’s agreement not to assert defenses when the assignee took for value, in good faith, without notice of a property or possessory claim to the assigned property, and without notice of specified defenses or recoupment claims. It preserved defenses available against a holder in due course. A qualifying assignee thus received analogous protection; the lease did not itself become a negotiable instrument. An account could also consist of a payment right not yet earned by performance.

Wells Fargo met all four conditions. The official comments contemplated enforcement even where other law would prevent enforcement by the assignor. The court therefore did not resolve the case merely by calling one statute more specific; the account assignment and directly applicable comments answered the question.

sections.title: The court evaluates the asserted defects in the papers
sections.cue: Keep the protection tied to this transaction.
paragraphs: The court also considered who could have prevented misleading papers from entering commerce. B.C.B.U. could have refused to sign an acceptance certificate contrary to reality and its express warning. Wells Fargo could not discover that the apparently finished transaction remained incomplete. That supported protection for this qualified purchaser, not immunity for all assignees.

Schedule A was in the file but not physically attached to the several documents referencing it. The trial court found that arrangement neither unusual nor notice of a defense, and the appellate court found no unsupported evidentiary finding. Failure of consideration was not a defense effective against a protected holder in due course. Ordinary contractual defenses and the narrower preserved defenses were not interchangeable, and no recoupment defense was suggested.

The asserted absence of mutual assent and material alteration also failed on these facts. Bangerter had knowingly signed the papers; the court expressly reserved a hypothetical forgery case. Calling an altered agreement void did not make its object or consideration illegal, and neither form of illegality was asserted here.

The acceptance certificate itself was properly admitted. The parties stipulated that Bangerter signed in his authorized corporate capacity. Whether an unattached schedule affected legal consequences was different from authenticity, and admitting the document fell within the trial judge’s discretion.

sections.title: Rescission cannot substitute for protected modification or payment
sections.cue: Explain why the original parties’ later cancellation did not discharge the assignee’s claim.
paragraphs: Section 9405 protected specified good-faith modifications or substitutions, giving an assignee corresponding rights under the changed agreement. Rescission left no replacement rights and therefore did not fit that protection. The court acknowledged that reducing payments to one dollar could resemble rescission economically, but good faith would still constrain that hypothetical modification. It did not authorize the parties to extinguish this assigned contract.

Section 9406 likewise allowed a debtor, before authenticated assignment notice, to discharge an obligation by paying the assignor. It did not validate every dealing with the assignor. B.C.B.U.’s claim that January 2001 cancellation worked because notice arrived only in January 2003 substituted cancellation for the required payment.

The Court of Appeal affirmed September 27, 2006, with appellate costs to Wells Fargo. An October 27 modification addressed a new argument that § 9403 became operative July 1, 2001, after the assignment. The rehearing petition was seven days late and the point had not previously been raised; additionally, former § 9206 provided the same relevant waiver and holder-in-due-course rule. Rehearing was denied and the judgment unchanged. No equipment delivery, forgery ruling, or recovery from Crocker was ordered.
